title: How to Use a HELOC to Buy Investment Property (Step-by-Step Guide)
excerpt: A Home Equity Line of Credit can be one of the most powerful—and underused—tools for funding your next real estate deal. Learn exactly how to use a HELOC to buy investment property, including real numbers, common pitfalls, and smart strategies.

sections.content: You might be sitting on more investment capital than you realize—locked inside the walls of your own home. A Home Equity Line of Credit, or HELOC, lets you tap into that equity and put it to work in real estate without selling your property or refinancing your entire mortgage. For investors looking to move fast and avoid large down payments from savings, learning how to use a HELOC to buy investment property can be a genuine game-changer. If you're newer to real estate financing in general, start with our [How to Finance Real Estate Investments: Complete Guide](aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-financing) before diving in here.
What Is a HELOC and How Does It Work?

A HELOC is a revolving line of credit secured by the equity in your primary residence or another property you own. Think of it like a credit card, but backed by your home and with much lower interest rates—typically between 7% and 10% as of 2024, depending on your credit score and lender. You draw money when you need it, pay it back, and draw again. Most HELOCs have a draw period of 5 to 10 years, followed by a repayment period of 10 to 20 years.

Lenders generally allow you to borrow up to 80% to 85% of your home's appraised value, minus what you still owe on your mortgage. Here's a quick example: if your home is worth $400,000 and you owe $200,000, you have $200,000 in equity. At 80% combined loan-to-value, the lender might approve a HELOC of up to $120,000. That $120,000 could be your down payment—or even your entire purchase price—on a rental property or fix-and-flip.
Why Investors Love Using a HELOC for Real Estate

items: Speed: Once approved, you can access funds in days—critical when competing for off-market deals.
Flexibility: Only borrow what you need, when you need it. No lump-sum pressure.
Lower cost than hard money: HELOC rates are usually 3%–6% lower than hard money loan rates.
Revolving access: Pay it back after a flip or refinance, then use it again on your next deal.
Interest-only payments: Most HELOCs allow interest-only payments during the draw period, improving short-term cash flow.
No prepayment penalties: Pay it off early with no fees when your deal closes.

sections.content: 'Your primary residence isn't just a place to live—it's a financial asset. Investors who understand that build portfolios twice as fast as those who don't.' — A common refrain among experienced real estate mentors
Step-by-Step: How to Use a HELOC to Buy Investment Property
Step 1: Determine Your Available Equity

Start by getting a rough appraisal or using online valuation tools to estimate your home's current market value. Subtract your outstanding mortgage balance. Multiply the result by 0.80 (most lenders cap at 80% LTV) and subtract the mortgage balance again—that's your rough HELOC ceiling. Call your bank or a credit union to get pre-qualified. Credit unions often offer better rates than big banks, so shop around before committing.
Step 2: Get Your HELOC Approved Before You Need It

Don't wait until you find a deal to apply. The approval process typically takes 2 to 6 weeks and requires a home appraisal, income verification, and a credit check. Most lenders want a credit score of at least 680, a debt-to-income ratio under 43%, and documented income. Apply early so that when the right deal appears, your line of credit is ready to deploy immediately.

Pro Tip: Apply for your HELOC during a slow market or before you actively start searching for deals. Lenders may freeze or reduce HELOCs during economic downturns, so securing your line early protects your access to capital when you need it most.
Step 3: Find the Right Investment Property

Your HELOC funds need to work hard enough to cover the interest cost and still generate profit. Before drawing a single dollar, run the numbers on every potential deal. Use our free [Deal Calculator](aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to quickly analyze purchase price, estimated repairs, after-repair value, and projected returns. Active investor markets like [Dallas, TX](aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), [Atlanta, GA](aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), and [Charlotte, NC](aiwholesail.com/markets/charlotte-nc) offer strong deal flow and solid appreciation potential for HELOC-funded acquisitions.
Step 4: Use the HELOC Strategically—Not as a Down Payment Trap

There are two common ways investors deploy a HELOC. The first is using it as a down payment on a conventional investment loan—for example, drawing $50,000 from your HELOC to cover the 20% down payment on a $250,000 rental property, then financing the rest with a traditional mortgage. The second approach is using the HELOC as your entire purchase price on a low-cost property, buying it outright, then refinancing into a long-term loan and paying the HELOC back—a strategy sometimes called BRRRR (Buy, Rehab, Rent, Refinance, Repeat). Learn more about the refinance piece in our [Cash-Out Refinance for Investors: When and How](aiwholesail.com/blog/cash-out-refinance-investors) article.
Step 5: Replenish and Repeat

The real power of a HELOC isn't a one-time shot—it's the cycle. You draw funds, acquire a property, stabilize or flip it, then pay the HELOC back. Now your line is open again for the next deal. Each completed deal potentially adds to your net worth and, if values rise, could even qualify you for a higher HELOC limit over time. Some investors run two or three cycles per year using a single HELOC.
HELOC vs. Other Real Estate Financing Options

A HELOC isn't the right tool for every situation. If you don't yet own a home with sufficient equity, you'll need to look elsewhere. [Hard money loans](aiwholesail.com/blog/hard-money-loans-explained) are a popular alternative—they're faster to close and don't require home equity, but they come with higher rates (10%–15%) and fees (2–4 points). For wholesalers who need short-term capital to close a double-close, [transactional funding](aiwholesail.com/blog/transactional-funding-wholesale) is typically a better fit. And for long-term investors with existing rental properties, a cash-out refinance may unlock more capital than a HELOC while locking in a fixed rate.
Risks to Know Before You Draw

items: Your home is collateral: If the deal goes bad and you can't repay, your primary residence is at risk.
Variable interest rates: Most HELOCs have adjustable rates, which can rise and increase your holding costs.
Lender freeze risk: Banks can reduce or freeze your HELOC during market downturns—even if you haven't missed a payment.
Over-leverage danger: Borrowing against your home to fund speculative deals can create a dangerous debt spiral.
Carry costs add up: Every month the HELOC is outstanding, interest accrues. Deals that drag on kill your margins.

sections.content: The best protection against these risks is solid deal analysis. Never deploy HELOC funds on a deal you haven't fully underwritten. Run your comps, estimate your rehab costs conservatively, and know your exit strategy before you draw a single dollar. For a deeper dive into deal analysis, check out our guide on [How to Analyze Real Estate Deals](aiwholesail.com/guides/how-to-analyze-real-estate-deals). And if you're just getting started with real estate investing, our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) guide walks you through the fundamentals of finding and profiting from your first deals.
A Real-World Example

Let's say you live in Charlotte, NC, and your home is worth $450,000 with a $220,000 mortgage balance. Your lender approves a HELOC up to $140,000. You find a distressed property listed at $115,000 that needs $25,000 in repairs and has an ARV of $195,000. You draw $115,000 from your HELOC to buy it cash, then use $25,000 of your own savings for renovations. After 90 days, you refinance the property with a rental loan at 75% LTV ($146,250), pay back the HELOC in full, and pocket roughly $6,250 while now owning a cash-flowing rental with no money left in the deal. That's the HELOC cycle in action.
